newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Europe marks 50th anniversary of Marshall Plan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe marks 50th anniversary of Marshall Plan.

text.p: When George C. Marshall outlined his plan for European recovery to graduates at Harvard University on June 5, 1947, Europe's industry was in tatters and its population faced hunger and disease in the wake of World War Two.

When President Bill Clinton addresses European leaders at a ceremony to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan next Wednesday, he will be speaking to representatives of some of the most powerful trading nations in the world -- a legacy of the huge transfer of aid from the United States to Europe after the war.

Clinton will be in the Netherlands next week for one of the biannual meetings scheduled with the European Union presidency, currently held by the Dutch, and is to combine his visit with a Marshall Plan commemoration.

At the heart of the commemoration will be an address by Clinton to representatives of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which groups the United Nations and Canada with European nations, spanning the northern hemisphere from Vancouver to Vladivostok.
HISTORIANS DIFFER ON U.S. MOTIVES

Historians dispute whether the plan, which saw the transfer of more than $12 billion in aid programmes to 16 European countries, was more in the interests of the United States or of Europe, and whether its motivation was more political than economic.
But one thing is clear as more countries press to join the European Union -- the principles of co-operation embedded in the plan were a blueprint for future international agreements.

Marshall, U.S. Secretary of State when he outlined his plan, set in motion a process which delivered the equivalent of around one percent of U.S. Gross Domestic Product to Europe between 1948 and 1952.
At current rates, bankers say the $12 billion transferred would be worth roughly $80 billion.

At the end of that period, total production in the target countries was more than 65 percent higher than at the start, national per capita incomes were more than 10 percent above pre-war levels, while economic growth rates exploded.

Marshall insisted that aid be tied to economic co-operation between the countries of Europe. This stipulation led to the creation of the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) to administer the plan in 1948 and played a part in the Soviet Union turning its back on it.

Donald Johnston, Secretary-General of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the direct successor to the OEEC, believes the Marshall Plan had lessons for the world and not just Europe.

"That legacy was the foresight of those who realised that lasting peace, prosperity and security may be defended through military prowess, but can only be acquired through economic development and co-operation," he said in a recent speech.
One historical perception of the Marshall Plan is that American generosity raised a crippled Europe from its knees and laid the foundations of its current prosperity.
DID MARSHALL PLAN SEEK TO HALT COMMUNISM?

Some historians take issue, arguing that Europe would have recovered after the war anyway and that the United States was serving its own interests by boosting markets for its own goods. It was also looking to head off the threat of Soviet communism with financial aid.

"The programme itself was economic but the motivation was primarily a political one -- to make sure Western Europe did not fall into the hands of Stalin," said Dutch historian Pieke van der Hoeven, an authority on the Marshall Plan.
She said communist movements were strong in many European countries after the war, in part because of the role their members had played in resisting Nazi Germany.
"At that time communists held around a third of the votes in France. The threat that communism would spread over Western Europe was not an imaginary danger," she said in an interview.

Van der Hoeven said the timing of the Marshall Plan had been vital because years of faltering postwar growth would have triggered social instability, exposing Europe to fresh waves of upheaval and conflict.
"Economic motives were there but a primary motivation was fear of Stalinism and another depression during which Europe would fall into communism," Van der Hoeven added.

"Europe has paid back America by being a healthy economy, by providing a market for their goods, but also there were parts given as loans which were paid back. It was in their interests politically and economically."

Marc Dierikx, another Netherlands-based Marshall Plan historian, said there was a school of thought which said the plan had significant benefits for the United States, which had to find jobs for demobilised troops and re-gear its industry away from war-time production.
"The Marshall Plan was a brilliant combination of various aims. I think that a considerable part of the Marshall Plan was rooted in U.S. domestic problems and policies," he said.

However historians pick over the legacies and motivations of the Plan, Eastern European leaders present at the Hague celebrations on May 28 can only rue the fact that Stalin and the Soviet Union blocked the eastward spread of Marshall aid.

Polish banker and opposition politician Andrzej Olechowski, who has been both finance and foreign minister since the 1989 fall of communism in his country, sees the Soviet Union's late 1940s order to Poland to refuse Marshall aid as a golden opportunity thrown away.
"This was a stupid ideological and unreasonable refusal. We lost a generation's worth of growth and welfare and this is what we now have to cover with our own effort.

"I'm afraid that was a unique opportunity and it is not going to be repeated in history, although Poland got some partial equivalent in the form of debt reduction after we changed the system," he told Reuters.

Western Europe is now seeking ways to increase involvement with its eastern neighbours, both through EU and NATO enlargement, binding the region in an ever more closely-knit economic and security bloc.

The Amsterdam EU summit next month is set to streamline decision-making in the 15-member bloc in readiness to welcome new partners from the east, following through on its extensive aid to central and eastern Europe.
Dutch Central Bank president Wim Duisenberg, in a recent speech, warned against viewing the Marshall Plan as a blueprint for aid to transforming economies in Central and Eastern Europe.

"The discussion in Eastern Europe is not so much about rebuilding existing structures, but rather about replacing them by new ones," said Duisenberg, adding that aid should be provided on the basis of actions taken by recipients rather than need.

But, putting the scale of the U.S. aid effort between 1948 and 1952 into perspective, he said: "If industrial countries were to make a similar effort and transfer one percent of their GDP to Eastern Europe, aid flows to this region would amount to more than $170 billion a year."
